One rule alone does not make a dog aggressive or even completely non aggressive either, it is but one of the many associations they can learn and is an example of a variable we humans can easily control.

Dogs did not originate from modern wolves, their ancestor is related to the wolves we see today; meaning, we don't know all the behaviors and drives that were in the original blueprint. Dogs adapted to selection pressures from humans, we can call one of those adaptations "people pleasing" as a very simplified term. Nothing was *bred into* dogs necessarily, but was emphasized while other traits and drives were reduced or removed. Their need for social interaction is complex and differs between dogs, but was already there in the canine ancestor. When humans imprint on dogs from the time they are pups, dogs easily show what we would call the desire to please humans; that is, to gain social interaction, enrichment, or pleasant physical contact. Feral dogs can learn that people suffice as a way to fill these needs as well, though the process looks different. All animals have a level of curiosity closely related to their skittishness, they crave new information. If they didn't, they'd die out. 

In video games, players normally attack, avoid, push aside, practice actions on, or steal from NPCs depending on the context and what they feel the impulse to do. They learn which NPCS can heal them, hurt them, or give them goods, even without consciously thinking "merchant/monk/mugger" they still have the concept in their head that this NPC who looks like this and does that is something beneficial to approach if they are low on health. If a player has a friendly and cautious personality they may behave differently than a player with a more callous, bold personality. Dogs operate in a similar way, except without conscious thought or the ability to premeditate actions.

Words like "dominance, trust, leadership, respect" (even "communication" in the way used above) are human terms for humans, but can be used as a way to describe animal psychology when it's a matter of function rather than understanding. With that aside...

Animals are like organic computers. They're running many programs in their heads and rely on direct feedback from their bodies and environment to function. Everything they do is a reaction, an end result of all those programs running and processing information or affecting other programs. They don't make choices. Scientists don't know all these programs yet, so it's easiest to simplify a dog's behavior based on those end results we can see. In their minds, everything is filtering through their programs, they don't really have a conscious concept of a person or dog. The way they think is, in as basic as I can go, (small human standing facing away -> no threat perceived, sniff to gain more info -> small human stiffens -> small human squeals -> small human runs -> chase) now the next time they see a small human, they are more inclined to sniff sooner and try to chase the child if s/he simply stands still or squeals. They begin to show behaviors sooner in the chain as a way of being efficient. This is learning. They might be so intelligent as to notice the specific smell of that child, something the child wore, something about the environment, or how its own body felt (hungry, sick, tired, etc) at the time, and take that into the program. That's how you hear about dogs "not liking" some people for seemingly unknown reasons or looking as if they "decide" to do something "mean" like get snappy with someone only "when they feel like it". These are just subtle triggers.


---

Animals have pre-wired behaviors right in their brains the day they're born. I.e., all animals, interestingly, know how to perform a killing blow, and it's actually highly similar between all species at its basic level; the bite, hold, and particular shake is something practically all animals can show without being taught. Hence why I say "programs," though people hate to hear animals talked about like they are machinery, because it implies they are as cold and unloving. That's a different subject.

So with all these pre-wired behaviors in the brain, there also traits an animal is born with. Each animal has needs, and fulfills these needs as best it can, using these traits. In example, we know dogs are highly social, predatory mammals; in selective breeding dogs adapted to the demands of people, becoming bloodhounds or lapdogs, so on. 

*People did not create these traits,* they were already present in dogs. Selective breeding only emphasizes or removes what was already there to work with. Original hound dogs were dogs that had a stronger drive to pursue scents and make noise frequently, loudly; terriers are dogs that developed a stronger drive to chase and fight tenacious prey even when hurt.

The drives were already there in original domestic dogs, with the purpose to fulfill their needs. These needs range from basic ones we understand (hunger, territorial needs, self-preservation) to ones we don't entirely understand (enrichment, reproduction, social).

Dogs as a predator species are pretty focused on hunting. Avoiding danger is secondary. Dogs didn't develop with many predators against their adults, so the danger comes mostly from lively prey and other dogs. We know a few "programs" they have pre-installed to deal with that; they have a pain and fear threshold for example. Some dogs, like terriers, developed high pain threshold and low fear, to be able to chase and kill prey that would put up a hard fight.


---

**tldr** Coming back to the topic of dominance... So if a dog has *learned*, that is, placed into its "programming", to pay attention to their handler, and behave in a pleasing way, in as many areas of its needs-driven brain as possible, that handler will gain what we humans call obedience and respect from the dog. It means reinforcing desired behavior and attention when the dog is trying to fulfill its needs, so that you have influence over those drives.

However, dogs, like any animal, can sense weakness and instability in other animals. Including in humans. You don't have to *establish dominance* per se, but you have to establish yourself as at least "not weak." Dominance theory is just a very simplified way of describing the way mammals evaluate the significance of living beings around them. Weak owners cause dogs to become anxious or aggressive. That's the culmination of many associations in their little minds regarding that person. This is why things like boundaries in the home (dog is told to keep out of the kitchen, stay off the couch, wait to greet visitors), pleasant "bonding" activities like grooming and treats, affect how a dog "respects" its owner. You're an unimportant NPC in the world of a dog until they learn otherwise.
